name: jesus-in-his-own-words.json
content:
Christian devotional writing often gathers verses into a list of what the believer is "in Christ": accepted, secure, significant, a child of God, "one spirit" with the Lord. Nearly every line of such lists comes from the letters of Paul. This page makes a different list. It sets down what ʿĪsā ibn Maryam (ʿalayhi al-salām, peace be upon him) said about himself and about God, in the Gospels the churches themselves accept, and then sets beside it what Paul said about him. The two portraits are not the same man. One is a servant of God who prays, obeys, does not know the hour and calls God "my God". The other is a heavenly being in the form of God, by whom all things were made. The first is the Messiah of the Gospels and of the Qurʾān. The second is the Christ of Paul.

"The Lord our God, the Lord is one"

Asked which commandment came first of all, ʿĪsā did not name himself, or a Trinity, or faith in his death. He recited the creed of Israel.

[paulus_figure name="galilee-green-hills"]Grassy slopes above the Sea of Galilee, the country where ʿĪsā taught (Mark 1:14–15).[/paulus_figure]

28And one of the scribes came up and heard them disputing with one another, and seeing that he answered them well, asked him, "Which commandment is the most important of all?" 29Jesus answered, "The most important is, 'Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. 30And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.'1

These are the words of Deuteronomy 6:4, the Shema, which every observant Jew of his day recited morning and evening: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one".2 ʿĪsā called it the first of all the commandments, and said "our God", counting himself among those who worship. The scribe repeated it back to him, adding that God is one "and there is no other besides him", and ʿĪsā told him he was "not far from the kingdom of God".3 The scribe confessed one God and was told that he was close.

When Satan offered him the kingdoms of the world in return for worship, ʿĪsā answered with the same law: "Be gone, Satan! For it is written, 'You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.'"4 Him only. He did not add "and me".

"Why do you call me good?"

A man ran up to ʿĪsā, knelt, and called him "Good Teacher". The answer he received is one of the most uncomfortable verses in the Gospels for the doctrine that ʿĪsā is God.

17And as he was setting out on his journey, a man ran up and knelt before him and asked him, "Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?" 18And Jesus said to him, "Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.5

Matthew, writing later and using Mark, softened the exchange. In his version the man asks "what good deed must I do", and ʿĪsā answers "Why do you ask me about what is good?" The King James text kept the Markan question, "Why callest thou me good?", but the oldest manuscripts of Matthew read as the ESV does. The change shows that the plain sense of Mark troubled the copyists too. Whatever else the words mean, they draw a line between ʿĪsā and the one God who alone is good, and ʿĪsā stands on the near side of it.

"The only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent"

The Gospel of John gives ʿĪsā the most exalted language of the four, and it is to John that missionaries go for "I and the Father are one". Yet John also preserves the prayer in which ʿĪsā defines eternal life itself:

3And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.7

There are two in this sentence: the only true God, and the one He sent. The God ʿĪsā prays to is "the only true God"; ʿĪsā himself is His messenger. This is the shape of the Muslim testimony of faith, which names God and then His messenger, and it is the shape of the Qurʾān's description of ʿĪsā: "The Messiah, Jesus the son of Mary, was but a messenger of Allāh".8

The oneness John speaks of is a oneness ʿĪsā prays his disciples may share: "that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us".9 No one takes the disciples to be God because of it. When his opponents accused him of making himself God, his reply in John was to cite Psalm 82, where the judges of Israel are called "gods", and to ask why they objected "because I said, 'I am the Son of God'".10 A "son of God", in the language of the Hebrew Bible, was a servant God had chosen: Israel, its kings, its righteous. Ismaʿil Raji al Faruqi made the point about "I and the Father are one": "Any righteous person could claim what Jesus did," he wrote, "in the sense of total compliance with God's will." The Semitic titles his disciples gave him, mar and maran, "lord" and "our lord", were used "among Semites" of "anyone in authority"; it was the Christians who came after them who took the titles as proof that he was God.11

In Divine Transcendence and Its Expression al Faruqi named the man who took that step. When the disciples call ʿĪsā "Lord", he wrote, it is a form of address "which implies respect and honor but not divinity, since it can be and is usually applied to any honored man. If Paul and other men with Hellenized minds misunderstood the term as meaning God, the fact tells about him, not about Jesus." The same is true of sonship: "It is only in John's Gospel and Paul's Epistles that 'sonship' becomes something mysterious and metaphysical."12

"my Father and your Father, to my God and your God"

After the empty tomb, in John's account, ʿĪsā sends Mary Magdalene to the disciples with a message about where he is going.

17Jesus said to her, "Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father; but go to my brothers and say to them, 'I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.'"13

Even in the Gospel that calls him the Word, at the end of the story, ʿĪsā has a God, and it is the same God as his disciples'. He calls them his brothers. The Qurʾān reports him saying exactly this to the Children of Israel:

إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ رَبِّى وَرَبُّكُمْ فَٱعْبُدُوهُ ۗ هَـٰذَا صِرَٰطٌ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ

"Indeed, Allāh is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. That is the straight path."14

The servant who does not know the hour

Again and again the Gospels show ʿĪsā depending on God for what he knows and does. "I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me."15 "The Father is greater than I."16 And of the day of judgment:

[paulus_figure name="twisted-olive-tree"]An ancient olive tree of the kind that grows on the Mount of Olives, where ʿĪsā went to pray: “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:39–42).[/paulus_figure]

32But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.17

One who does not know the hour is not all-knowing. One who can do nothing of himself is not all-powerful. One who says that another is greater than he is does not claim to be his equal. The church answered these verses with the doctrine of two natures, a divine one that knew and a human one that did not, worked out at Chalcedon in 451, four centuries after ʿĪsā spoke. He himself never offered it. He spoke as a servant, and in Gethsemane he prayed as one: "My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will."18 Two wills, and he submits his to God's. That is what the Arabic word islām means.

"A man who has told you the truth"

ʿĪsā described himself in John as "a man who has told you the truth that I heard from God".19 Peter, preaching in Jerusalem at Pentecost in the first public sermon Acts records, described him the same way.

22Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know—20

A man, approved of God; the miracles are God's, done through him. This is the Christology of the disciples who had walked with him, and it is the Christology of the Qurʾān, in which ʿĪsā heals the blind and the leper and raises the dead "by permission of Allāh".21 When ʿĪsā asked his disciples who they said he was, Peter answered, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God".22 He did not answer "You are God".

What Paul said about him

Paul never met ʿĪsā in his lifetime and quotes almost none of his teaching. What he offers instead is a heavenly figure, revealed to him in visions. In a hymn in Philippians he describes Christ as one "who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped", and then applies to him a verse of Isaiah in which God swears by Himself, "To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear allegiance".23 In Paul's hymn the knees bow "at the name of Jesus", and the tongues confess "that Jesus Christ is Lord". Words that Isaiah reserved for the God of Israel are transferred to a man.

[paulus_figure name="open-bible-lit"]An open Bible. Philippians 2:6 and Colossians 1:15 are the verses set beside the words of ʿĪsā.[/paulus_figure]

The letter to the Colossians, which many scholars believe was written in Paul's name after his death, goes further.

15He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation. 16For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities—all things were created through him and for him.24

"For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily," the same letter says.25 Set this beside the man in Mark who will not be called good, who does not know the hour, and who names the Shema as the first commandment. The creator of thrones and dominions is not a figure ʿĪsā ever described. The steps by which Paul raised him, from "Lord" to a heavenly being close to an angel, are traced in [paulus_link slug="lord-before-the-spirit" /] and [paulus_link slug="seven-doctrines" /].

The title Paul gives him, "the image of the invisible God", is itself a step away from the Gospels. Luke's genealogy traces ʿĪsā back through Ādam, "the son of God".26 Al Faruqi observed that Luke thereby granted Ādam, "and all mankind after him, an even higher status than that of 'image of God'", which "contrasts sharply with Paul's use of this notion for the characterization of Jesus."27 In Luke, every child of Ādam is a child of God in this sense, and ʿĪsā shares the title with all of them. Paul made "the image of God" a title for one man alone.

The Qurʾān on ʿĪsā

The Qurʾān honours ʿĪsā more than many Christians expect. It names him the Messiah, the Word of God and a spirit from Him, born of a virgin, a worker of miracles, raised up by God. What it refuses is the step Paul took. Its first words from ʿĪsā, spoken from the cradle, are these:

قَالَ إِنِّى عَبْدُ ٱللَّهِ ءَاتَىٰنِىَ ٱلْكِتَـٰبَ وَجَعَلَنِى نَبِيًّا

"[Jesus] said, 'Indeed, I am the servant of Allāh. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet.'"28

On the Day of Judgment, the Qurʾān says, God will ask ʿĪsā whether he told people to take him and his mother as gods besides God, and he will answer: "Exalted are You! It was not for me to say that to which I have no right. … I said not to them except what You commanded me — to worship Allāh, my Lord and your Lord."29 The Qurʾān's ʿĪsā and the ʿĪsā of Mark and John say the same thing about who God is. Only Paul's Christ says otherwise, and Paul's Christ never spoke in the Gospels at all.

In short

  • ʿĪsā named the Shema, "The Lord our God, the Lord is one", as the first commandment (Mark 12:29).
  • He refused to be called good, since "No one is good except God alone" (Mark 10:18).
  • He called the God he prayed to "the only true God" and himself the one sent (John 17:3).
  • He had a God, the same as his disciples' (John 20:17), and did not know the hour (Mark 13:32).
  • Peter called him "a man attested to you by God" (Acts 2:22).
  • Paul made him one "in the form of God", and Colossians the creator of all things (Philippians 2:6; Colossians 1:16).
  • The Qurʾān's ʿĪsā says "I am the servant of Allāh" (Maryam 19:30).

How ʿĪsā taught his disciples to pray, and to whom, is on [paulus_link slug="the-prayer-jesus-taught" /]. What he taught about sin and forgiveness is on [paulus_link slug="original-sin" /].
